title: Longest Join of Letter-Distinct Words
statement:
You get a list of lowercase words. Pick some of them (any subset, possibly none) and glue them together in their original order. The glued string must not use any letter more than once.

Return the length of the longest string you can build this way. A word that repeats a letter inside itself can never be picked.

examples.why: "ab" + "cd" = "abcd". "ace" shares a letter with each of the others, so on its own it only reaches 3.
"xyz" + "qw". "yy" repeats a letter, so it is never usable.
Taking the longest word first gives "abcd" + "fg" = 6. Skipping it allows "ab" + "cde" + "fg" = 7.

constraints: words[i] holds only lowercase English letters
hints: With at most 16 words there are at most 2¹⁶ subsets. How can you explore them while cutting off branches early?
Represent each word's letters as a 26-bit mask. Two words clash exactly when their masks share a bit, which is one &.
Backtrack over the words in order: either skip word i, or take it if its mask does not overlap the current mask. Drop words with a repeated letter before starting.

explain.intuition:
There is no greedy rule here: taking the longest word can block two shorter words that together are longer (example 3). With only 16 words, though, trying every subset is affordable, as long as each check is cheap.

A bitmask makes it cheap. Each word becomes a 26-bit number with one bit per letter. A word clashes with the current selection exactly when mask & wordMask ≠ 0, and adding it is mask | wordMask. A word that repeats a letter inside itself is thrown away up front. Then a short backtracking search either takes or skips each word, pruning any branch that would clash.
steps: Turn each word into a letter mask. Skip words whose letters repeat (the mask has fewer bits than the word has letters).
Backtrack with dfs(i, mask): record popcount(mask) as a candidate answer.
For each later word j ≥ i whose mask does not overlap mask, recurse into dfs(j + 1, mask | m[j]).
pitfalls: Greedily taking the longest compatible word first. Example 3 shows it loses.
Forgetting that a single word can itself repeat a letter, like "yy".
Comparing words letter by letter at every step instead of with masks, which multiplies the work by 26.

complexity.time: O(2ⁿ) subsets, O(1) each with masks

solutions.title: Every subset with string checks
solutions.idea: Enumerate all 2ⁿ subsets, glue the chosen words and test the result with a set.

solutions.title: Backtracking with letter masks
solutions.idea: Each word is a 26-bit mask. Only extend with words whose mask does not overlap the current one.

solutions.title: Set of reachable masks
solutions.idea: Keep the set of all letter masks you can build so far. Each new word extends every compatible mask.

followups: Return the chosen words, not just the length. If several choices tie, which one would you report?
There are 1 000 words but only 26 letters. Why does the number of distinct reachable masks stay manageable in practice?
lcTitle: Maximum Length of a Concatenated String with Unique Characters
